Storage.FC1.name: Storage account
Storage.FC1.description: Azure Storage is Microsoft's Cloud Storage solution for modern data storage scenarios. Azure Storage offers a scalable object store for data objects, a file system service for the cloud, a messaging store for reliable messaging, and a NoSQL store.

Storage.FC2.name: Blob storage
Storage.FC2.description: Object storage solution for storing unstructured data (blobs) accessible via HTTP/S and optionally via the Network File System (NFS) v3 and SFTP protocols.

Storage.FC3.name: File shares
Storage.FC3.description: Azure Files offers fully governed file shares in the cloud accessible via Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, Network File System (NFS) v4.1 protocol, or the in-preview Azure Files REST API.

Storage.FC4.name: Queues
Storage.FC4.description: Azure Queue Storage is a service for storing messages. Access messages via HTTP/S calls.

Storage.FC5.name: Tables
Storage.FC5.description: Azure table storage is a service that stores non-relational structured data (or structured NoSQL data) in the cloud, providing a key/attribute store with a schemaless design.

Storage.FC10.name: Blob inventory
Storage.FC10.description: The Azure Storage blob inventory feature provides an overview of your containers, blobs, snapshots, and blob versions within a storage account. Use the inventory report to understand various attributes of blobs and containers, such as the total data size, age, encryption status, immutability policy, and legal hold.

Storage.FC11.name: Local users
Storage.FC11.description: Blob storage supports the SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP). This support lets you securely connect to blob storage via an SFTP endpoint, allowing you to use SFTP for file access, file transfer, and file management.

Storage.FC12.name: Private endpoints
Storage.FC12.description: Azure Storage private endpoint is a network interface that enables secure, private connectivity between Azure Storage and virtual networks using Azure Private Link, preventing exposure to the public internet and enhancing security.

Storage.T1.name: Credential access by listing or regenerating storage account access keys
Storage.T1.description: Storage account access keys provide broad authorization to storage account resources. An attacker can list, regenerate, or rotate storage account access keys to obtain a valid Shared Key and enable later unauthorized access to storage data.

Storage.T2.name: Service impact through regeneration of storage account access keys
Storage.T2.description: SAS tokens can be signed with a storage account access key, enabling applications to access storage account data. An attacker can rotate or regenerate a storage account access key to invalidate SAS tokens derived from that key, blocking access for applications that depend on those tokens.

Storage.T3.name: Unauthorized access to storage data using a compromised access key or SAS token
Storage.T3.description: Storage account access keys and Shared Access Signature tokens authorize access to storage resources based on the credential's effective scope. An attacker can use a compromised storage account access key, connection string, or SAS URL to read storage data outside the intended authorization path.

Storage.T4.name: Data manipulation through reuse of a deleted storage account name
Storage.T4.description: Azure Storage account names are globally unique and can be referenced by applications, users, or third parties. An attacker can delete a storage account and recreate a new storage account with the same name to host misleading, malicious, or attacker-controlled data at a previously trusted endpoint.

Storage.T5.name: Unauthorized access to blob data by enabling anonymous public access
Storage.T5.description: Azure blob containers can allow anonymous public access to blobs when account-level public access is permitted. An attacker can modify container public access settings to expose blob data outside the intended authorization path.

Storage.T7.name: Service impact through recursive deletion of hierarchical namespace content
Storage.T7.description: Azure Storage accounts with hierarchical namespace enabled can organize blob data into directories and files. An attacker can recursively delete directories or files to make stored content unavailable to legitimate users.

Storage.T8.name: Data manipulation through unauthorized modification of blob data
Storage.T8.description: Azure Blob Storage supports authorized access for creating, replacing, or modifying blob content. An attacker can modify blob data to alter stored content outside the intended authorization path.

Storage.T9.name: Encrypt blob contents for ransom using authorized access
Storage.T9.description: Azure Blob Storage can store file and object data that may be replaced through authorized blob access. An attacker can replace blob contents with encrypted data under their control and demand payment for recovery.

Storage.T12.name: Service impact through unauthorized modification of blob content
Storage.T12.description: Azure Blob Storage can host files consumed by users, applications, or downstream services. An attacker can replace blob contents with malicious or unauthorized content (e.g., malware), causing consumers of the blob to retrieve harmful content from a previously trusted storage location.

Storage.T13.name: Data exposure through storage account replication
Storage.T13.description: Azure Storage object replication can copy blobs, metadata, and tags from a source storage account to a destination storage account. An attacker can configure replication to copy storage data to an unauthorized destination, exposing replicated content outside the intended storage boundary.

Storage.T15.name: Unauthorized access to Azure file share contents
Storage.T15.description: Azure file shares can expose stored files through supported access methods (e.g., SMB, NFS, REST APIs). An attacker can browse exposed file shares to access and retrieve file contents (e.g., text files, Word documents, PDF files).

Storage.T16.name: Financial impact through unauthorized upload of Azure file share contents
Storage.T16.description: Azure file shares can incur storage and transaction costs based on stored file data and usage. An attacker can upload excessive file content to increase storage consumption and generate unexpected costs.

Storage.T17.name: Privilege escalation by modifying Azure file share permissions
Storage.T17.description: Azure file shares support file and directory permissions that control access to share content. An attacker can modify file or directory permissions to grant broader access to protected share content or enable later unauthorized operations.

Storage.T18.name: Service impact through recursive deletion of Azure file share contents
Storage.T18.description: Azure file shares can store files in hierarchical directory structures (e.g., project folders, user home directories, application data folders). An attacker can recursively delete directories or files in a file share, making stored content unavailable to legitimate users.

Storage.T19.name: Impact through unauthorized encryption of Azure file share contents
Storage.T19.description: Azure file shares store file content that can be accessed and modified through authorized file access. An attacker can overwrite or encrypt file contents in a file share to make the data unusable and demand payment for recovery.

Storage.T20.name: Distribute malicious content via unauthorized upload
Storage.T20.description: Azure file shares can host files consumed by users, applications, or mounted systems. An attacker can upload malicious or unauthorized content (e.g., scripts, executables, documents with embedded payloads), causing consumers of the file share to retrieve harmful content from a previously trusted storage location.

Storage.T22.name: Publish malicious content by modifying static website blobs
Storage.T22.description: Azure Storage static websites serve content from a blob storage container, named $web, over a web endpoint. An attacker can modify files in the $web container to publish malicious or unauthorized content through a trusted storage-hosted website.

Storage.T24.name: Blob inventory discovery through inventory access
Storage.T24.description: Blob inventory reports list blob objects, metadata, versions, and related storage details for a storage account. An attacker can access blob inventory reports to identify stored objects, naming patterns, and data locations for later targeted access.

Storage.T25.name: Service impact through lifecycle management changes
Storage.T25.description: Blob Storage lifecycle management applies rules that transition or expire blob data based on age, access, or metadata conditions. An attacker can modify lifecycle management rules to delete blob data or move it to colder tiers, reducing data availability or increasing recovery time.

Storage.T26.name: Data exposure through CORS configuration changes
Storage.T26.description: CORS settings control which browser-based origins can access Azure Storage service responses. An attacker can modify CORS rules for blob, queue, file, or table services to allow untrusted origins to access storage responses through a browser-based application flow.

Storage.T27.name: Privilege escalation through queue access policy modification
Storage.T27.description: Queue stored access policies can define permissions and constraints for Shared Access Signatures used with Azure Storage queues. An attacker can modify queue access policies to grant broader queue access than intended.

Storage.T28.name: Privilege escalation through table access policy modification
Storage.T28.description: Table stored access policies can define permissions and constraints for Shared Access Signatures used with Azure Storage tables. An attacker can modify table access policies to grant broader table access than intended.

Storage.T31.name: Service impact through queue message modification or deletion
Storage.T31.description: Azure Storage queues contain messages consumed by applications and downstream services. An attacker can modify, delete, or purge queue messages, causing downstream applications to process incorrect data or lose required work items.

Storage.T34.name: Financial impact through query acceleration usage
Storage.T34.description: Azure Storage query acceleration can process readable blob data using service-side query execution with a separate pricing model. An attacker can repeatedly execute query acceleration requests against readable blob data to generate unexpected processing costs.

Storage.T38.name: Service impact through encryption scope modification
Storage.T38.description: Azure Storage encryption scopes define the encryption settings and keys used to protect blob data. An attacker can modify an encryption scope to use a different key, causing future blob writes or updates under that scope to become inaccessible to users or resources that do not have access to the new key.

Storage.T39.name: Service impact through disabling blob soft delete
Storage.T39.description: Blob soft delete allows deleted blob data to be recovered during a configured retention period. An attacker can disable blob soft delete to reduce recovery options after later unauthorized deletion or overwrite of blob data.

Storage.T40.name: Impact of disabling blob versioning
Storage.T40.description: Blob versioning can be enabled for supported Azure Blob Storage accounts to preserve previous versions of blob data when blobs are modified or overwritten. An attacker can disable blob versioning on a supported storage account to prevent new versions from being created, reducing recovery options after later unauthorized modification or overwrite of blob data.

Storage.T42.name: Service impact through replication configuration changes
Storage.T42.description: Azure Storage replication helps preserve data availability and durability across storage locations. An attacker can modify replication configuration to reduce redundancy, weaken recovery options, or increase the impact of a regional failure.

Storage.T44.name: Persistent access through SFTP local user credentials
Storage.T44.description: Azure Storage accounts can support SFTP access through local user credentials. An attacker can create or modify SFTP local user credentials to maintain an alternate access path to storage data.

Storage.T48.name: Unauthorized access to blob data through overly permissive Azure RBAC assignments
Storage.T48.description: Azure Storage can authorize blob data access through Azure RBAC assignments that evaluate request, resource, environment, or principal attributes. An attacker can satisfy overly permissive or incorrectly scoped assignments to read blob data outside the intended authorization scope.

Storage.T50.name: Unauthorized access path through virtual network rule changes
Storage.T50.description: Storage account network settings can restrict access through public network access, firewall rules, IP rules, virtual network rules, and trusted service bypass settings. An attacker can modify storage account network configuration to allow access from unauthorized network paths, enabling later access to storage account resources.

Storage.T55.name: Unauthorized access to blob data by renaming a path used by Azure RBAC assignments
Storage.T55.description: Azure Storage can authorize blob data access through Azure RBAC assignments that evaluate blob path attributes. An attacker can rename or move a blob path to satisfy an overly permissive path-based assignment (ref) and read blob data outside the intended authorization scope.

Storage.T56.name: Impact by modifying blob container immutability protections
Storage.T56.description: Azure blob containers can use immutability policies and legal holds to prevent protected blob data from being modified or deleted. An attacker can modify immutability policy settings or legal hold state to weaken protection for blob data and enable later unauthorized modification or deletion.

Storage.T58.name: Unauthorized access to blob data through overly permissive hierarchical namespace ACLs
Storage.T58.description: Azure Storage accounts with hierarchical namespace enabled can authorize file and directory access using POSIX-like Access Control Lists. An attacker can use overly permissive hierarchical namespace ACLs to read blob data outside the intended authorization scope.

Storage.T59.name: Unauthorized failover through configuration change
Storage.T59.description: Azure Storage accounts support failover, which transitions geo-redundant storage accounts from their primary region to the secondary, deleting the original primary data and converting the account to locally redundant storage. An attacker can initiate an unauthorized failover to disrupt availability, cause loss of unreplicated data, degrade redundancy, and introduce inconsistencies due to asynchronous replication.

Storage.T60.name: Data exposure through file share encryption changes
Storage.T60.description: Azure file shares can support encryption settings for data in transit. An attacker can modify file share encryption settings to permit weaker or unencrypted connections, potentially exposing file share contents to interception while they are being accessed.

Storage.T61.name: Data exposure through legacy file share protocols
Storage.T61.description: Azure file shares can support legacy SMB protocol versions and encryption settings for compatibility with older clients (e.g., SMB 2.1, SMB 3.x without encryption, or weaker channel encryption settings). An attacker can modify file share protocol settings to permit weaker access methods, potentially exposing file share contents to protocol-level weaknesses or interception.

Storage.T62.name: Service impact through private endpoint deletion
Storage.T62.description: Azure Storage accounts can use private endpoints to provide private network access to storage services. An attacker can delete a private endpoint connection, disrupting private access paths used by legitimate clients.

Storage.T63.name: Data exposure through unauthorized replication policy
Storage.T63.description: Storage replication policies can continuously replicate blob data, metadata, and tags from a source storage account to a destination storage account. An attacker can configure an unauthorized replication policy to continuously copy storage data to an unauthorized destination, including a storage account in another subscription or tenant.

Storage.T64.name: Credential access through SMB Shared Key retrieval
Storage.T64.description: Azure file shares can support SMB access through local user credentials that include Shared Key material. An attacker can list local user keys to obtain SMB credentials and enable later file share access outside the intended authorization path.

Storage.T65.name: File share access through SMB Shared Key
Storage.T65.description: Azure file shares can support SMB authentication using Shared Key credentials. An attacker can use an obtained or compromised SMB Shared Key to mount or access the file share outside the intended authorization path.

Storage.T66.name: Privilege escalation through hierarchical namespace ACL modification
Storage.T66.description: Azure Storage accounts with hierarchical namespace enabled can authorize file and directory access using POSIX-like Access Control Lists. An attacker can modify hierarchical namespace ACLs to grant broader access to protected blob data.

Storage.T67.name: Unauthorized access to sensitive queue message contents
Storage.T67.description: Azure Storage queues can contain messages used by applications and downstream services. An attacker with queue message access can read, peek, or dequeue queue messages to access sensitive data, operational instructions, or workflow state outside the intended processing path.

Storage.T68.name: Public access path through account configuration
Storage.T68.description: Storage accounts can control whether blob containers are allowed to expose data through anonymous public access. An attacker can enable account-level public blob access, allowing containers to be configured for anonymous access and enabling later exposure of blob data.

Storage.T69.name: Shared Key access path through the account configuration
Storage.T69.description: Storage accounts can control whether requests are authorized with account access keys through Shared Key authorization. An attacker can enable Shared Key access on a storage account, allowing access keys or key-signed SAS tokens to authorize requests outside the intended identity-based authorization path.

Storage.A1.action_description: Registers the subscription for the storage resource provider and enables the creation of storage accounts.

Storage.A2.action_description: Notifies Azure Storage that a virtual network or subnet is being deleted.

Storage.A3.action_description: List blob services of a storage account. It returns a collection of one object named default.

Storage.A4.action_description: Retrieves a user delegation key for the blob service. This is only a valid operation when using bearer token authentication.

Storage.A5.action_description: Sets the properties of a storage account's blob service, including properties for storage Analytics and CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules.

Storage.A6.action_description: Gets the properties of a storage account's blob service, including properties for storage Analytics and CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules.

Storage.A7.action_description: Returns a list of blobs under the specified container.

Storage.A8.action_description: Creates a new block, page, or append blob, or updates the content of an existing block blob. The Put blob operation will overwrite all contents of an existing blob with the same name.

Storage.A9.action_description: Deletes the specified blob or snapshot. Note that in order to delete a blob, you must delete all of its snapshots. You can delete both at the same time with the "Delete blob" operation.

Storage.A10.action_description: Deletes a specific version of a blob without affecting other versions or the current blob.

Storage.A11.action_description: This operation allows for the permanent deletion of soft-deleted blob snapshots or versions before the retention period expires.

Storage.A12.action_description: Allows you to create a new blob or overwrite an existing blob within a container.

Storage.A13.action_description: Allows you to search for blobs within a container based on their assigned tags.

Storage.A14.action_description: Allows you to copy an existing blob to a new location within the same storage account or across different storage accounts.

Storage.A15.action_description: Allows you to set system properties on the blob, such as cache control, content type, and metadata.

Storage.A16.action_description: Manages access control and permissions for blobs within Azure Storage.

Storage.A18.action_description: This operation migrates a blob container from container-level WORM to an object-level immutability enabled container. Prerequisites require a container-level immutability policy either in a locked or unlocked state, account-level versioning must be enabled and there should be no legal hold on the container.

Storage.A19.action_description: Updates container properties as specified in the request body. Properties not mentioned in the request will be unchanged. The update fails if the specified container doesn't already exist.

Storage.A20.action_description: Deletes the specified container under its account.

Storage.A21.action_description: Gets the properties of a specified container.

Storage.A22.action_description: Lists all containers and does not support a prefix like data plane. Also SRP today does not return a continuation token.

Storage.A23.action_description: The Lease container operation establishes and manages a lock on a container for delete operations. The lock duration can be 15 to 60 seconds, or can be infinite.

Storage.A24.action_description: Creates a new container under the specified account as described by the request body. The container resource includes metadata and properties for that container. It does not include a list of the blobs contained by the container.

Storage.A25.action_description: Clears legal hold tags. Clearing the same or non-existing tag results in an idempotent operation. ClearLegalHold clears out only the specified tags in the request.

Storage.A26.action_description: Sets legal hold tags. Setting the same tag results in an idempotent operation. SetLegalHold follows an append pattern and does not clear out the existing tags that are not specified in the request.

Storage.A27.action_description: Extends the immutabilityPeriodSinceCreationInDays of a locked ImmutabilityPolicy. The only action allowed on a locked policy will be this action. ETag in If-Match is required for this operation.

Storage.A28.action_description: Aborts an unlocked immutability policy. The response of delete has immutabilityPeriodSinceCreationInDays set to 0. ETag in If-Match is required for this operation. Deleting a locked immutability policy is not allowed, the only way is to delete the container after deleting all expired blobs inside the policy-locked container.

Storage.A29.action_description: Creates or updates an unlocked immutability policy. ETag in If-Match is honored if given, but not required for this operation.

Storage.A30.action_description: Sets the ImmutabilityPolicy to locked state. The only action allowed on a locked policy is the ExtendImmutabilityPolicy action. ETag in If-Match is required for this operation.

Storage.A31.action_description: Gets the existing immutability policy along with the corresponding ETag in response headers and body.

Storage.A32.action_description: List all queue services for the storage account.

Storage.A33.action_description: Gets the properties of a storage account's queue service, including properties for storage Analytics and CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules.

Storage.A34.action_description: Sets the properties of a storage account's queue service, including properties for storage Analytics and CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules.

Storage.A35.action_description: Creates a new queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account. Creates a new queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account.

Storage.A36.action_description: Gets the queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account if it exists. Gets a list of all the queues under the specified storage account.

Storage.A37.action_description: Creates a new queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account. Creates a new queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account.

Storage.A38.action_description: Deletes the queue with the specified queue name, under the specified account if it exists.

Storage.A39.action_description: Retrieves one or more messages from the front of the queue.

Storage.A40.action_description: Adds a new message to the back of the message queue. A visibility time-out can also be specified to make the message invisible until the visibility time-out expires. A message must be in a format that can be included in an XML request with UTF-8 encoding. The encoded message can be up to 64 kibibytes (KiB) in size for version 2011-08-18 and later, or 8 KiB for earlier versions.

Storage.A41.action_description: Deletes the specified message from the queue.

Storage.A42.action_description: This operation allows you to add a new message to the back of a specified queue.

Storage.A43.action_description: Handles operations that involve processing messages in Azure Queue Storage. This encompasses actions such as retrieving messages from a queue, updating their visibility, and deleting them after processing.

Storage.A44.action_description: The update operation can be used to update the SKU, encryption, access tier, or tags for a storage account. It can also be used to map the account to a custom domain. Only one custom domain is supported per storage account; the replacement/change of custom domain is not supported.

Storage.A45.action_description: Live migration of storage account to enable HNS.

Storage.A46.action_description: Live migration of storage account to enable HNS.

Storage.A47.action_description: Restore blobs in the specified blob ranges.

Storage.A48.action_description: Used for approving or rejecting private endpoint connections for Azure Storage accounts.

Storage.A49.action_description: A failover request can be triggered for a storage account in the event a primary endpoint becomes unavailable for any reason. The failover occurs from the storage account's primary cluster to the secondary cluster for RA-GRS accounts. The secondary cluster will become primary after failover and the account is converted to LRS. In the case of a Planned failover, the primary and secondary clusters are swapped after failover and the account remains geo-replicated. Failover should continue to be used in the event of availability issues as Planned failover is only available while the primary and secondary endpoints are available. The primary use case of a Planned failover is Disaster Recovery testing drills. This type of failover is invoked by setting failoverType parameter to "Planned". Learn more about the failover options here- "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-disaster-recovery-guidance".

Storage.A50.action_description: Lists the access keys or Kerberos keys (if Active Directory enabled) for the specified storage account.

Storage.A51.action_description: Regenerates one of the access keys or Kerberos keys for the specified storage account.

Storage.A52.action_description: Used as part of the regenerate keys process.

Storage.A54.action_description: Deletes a storage account in Microsoft Azure.

Storage.A55.action_description: Lists all the storage accounts available under the subscription.

Storage.A56.action_description: List SAS credentials of a storage account.

Storage.A57.action_description: List service SAS credentials of a specific resource.

Storage.A58.action_description: Asynchronously creates a new storage account with the specified parameters. If an account is already created and a subsequent create request is issued with different properties, the account properties will be updated. If an account is already created and a subsequent create or update request is issued with the exact same set of properties, the request will succeed. The update operation can be used to update the SKU, encryption, access tier, or tags for a storage account.

Storage.A59.action_description: Configure monitoring and logging settings through Azure Resource Manager (ARM) APIs.

Storage.A60.action_description: Get list of Azure Storage metrics definitions.

Storage.A61.action_description: Gets the diagnostic setting for the resource.

Storage.A62.action_description: Creates or updates the diagnostic setting for the resource.

Storage.A63.action_description: Get a list of Azure Storage metrics definitions.

Storage.A64.action_description: Gets the diagnostic setting for the resource.

Storage.A164.action_description: If the storage account's soft delete feature is disabled, then when a blob is deleted, it is permanently removed from the storage account. If the storage account's soft delete feature is enabled, then when a blob is deleted, it is marked for deletion and becomes inaccessible immediately. However, the blob service retains the blob or snapshot for the number of days specified by the DeleteRetentionPolicy section of [storage service properties] (Set-blob-Service-Properties.md). After the specified number of days has passed, the blob's data is permanently removed from the storage account. Note that you continue to be charged for the soft-deleted blob's storage until it is permanently removed. Use the "List blobs" API and specify the "include=deleted" query parameter to discover which blobs and snapshots have been soft deleted. You can then use the "Undelete Blob" API to restore a soft-deleted blob. All other operations on a soft-deleted blob or snapshot cause the service to return an HTTP status code of 404 (ResourceNotFound).

Storage.A199.action_description: A failover request can be triggered for a storage account in the event a primary endpoint becomes unavailable for any reason. The failover occurs from the storage account's primary cluster to the secondary cluster for RA-GRS accounts. The secondary cluster will become primary after failover and the account is converted to LRS. In the case of a Planned failover, the primary and secondary clusters are swapped after failover and the account remains geo-replicated. Failover should continue to be used in the event of availability issues as Planned failover is only available while the primary and secondary endpoints are available. The primary use case of a Planned failover is Disaster Recovery testing drills. This type of failover is invoked by setting "FailoverType" parameter to "Planned". Learn more about the failover options here ref.
